title: 22. Interview: AI Agent Evaluation: Tasks, Tools, and Trajectories

objectives: Answer the AI Agent Evaluation: Tasks, Tools, and Trajectories interview questions out loud

sections.title: 11. Interview Questions
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual

**Q1.** What is the difference between step-level and end-state evaluation, and when is each more useful?

> End-state scoring checks only the final answer — fast, cheap, user-aligned. Step-level scoring checks every (state, action) pair — slow, expensive, but diagnostic. Use end-state for headline metrics, step-level for debugging failures.

**Q2.** Why is BLEU useless for evaluating an agent that writes and runs code?

> BLEU measures n-gram overlap between a candidate and a reference string. Agents produce trajectories (tool calls, observations, code edits), not strings. Two patches can be textually different yet behaviorally identical (same tests pass) or textually similar yet behaviorally different. The "right answer" is a passing test suite, not a string.

**Q3.** Define Tool Selection Accuracy. Why is it not enough on its own?

> TSA = (# steps where agent picked the right tool) / (total steps). It misses argument quality, execution success, and ordering. An agent can have TSA=1.0 and TSR=0.0 if every tool is correct but every argument is wrong.

**Q4.** What does SWE-bench measure that HumanEval does not, and why does that matter for coding agents?

> HumanEval checks whether a single function passes its own unit tests — a one-shot completion task. SWE-bench asks the agent to resolve a real GitHub issue in a real repo: locate the bug across multiple files, edit code, run the project's existing test suite. This exercises planning, navigation, and iteration — the actual work of a coding agent.

**Q5.** How would you evaluate an agent's reflection ability?

> Inject controlled errors (fail a tool call, return a malformed observation) at known points and measure whether the agent produces a correct recovery action within N steps. Reflection Success Rate = recovered errors / total injected errors.

**Q6.** Why do agents need human evaluation more than raw LLMs do?

> LLM outputs are short and self-contained — LLM-as-judge correlates well with humans. Agent trajectories are long, multi-criteria, and context-sensitive — judges lose context and miss subtle safety issues. Human eval is the only reliable ground truth for "was this trajectory reasonable?"

**Q7.** What is the difference between Path Efficiency and Trajectory Efficiency?

> PE = optimal_steps / actual_steps. It counts steps. TE = sequence similarity to an expert trajectory. It judges *which* steps. Two agents with PE=1.0 can have very different TE if one follows expert logic and the other takes a lucky shortcut.

**Q8.** Explain the four evaluation points in the agent loop.

> (1) Reasoning quality — was the planner's thought sound? (2) Tool selection — did it pick the right tool? (3) Argument quality — were the args correct? (4) End-state — did the task succeed? Each isolates a different failure mode.

**Q9.** What is per-tool precision vs recall, and why does aggregate TSA hide problems?

> Per-tool precision = (correct uses of tool X) / (all uses of tool X). Recall = (correct uses of X) / (times X was the right choice). Aggregate TSA can be 95% while recall on one critical tool is 30% — the agent simply avoids that tool entirely.

**Q10.** Why report cost-per-success rather than raw cost or raw TSR?

> A model that is cheap but fails often has low total cost but is useless. A model with high TSR but $5/task may not be viable. Cost-per-success merges both: how many dollars buys a correct task. It is the metric product teams actually optimize.

### B. Scenario-Based

**Scenario**: Your agent completes tasks successfully 90% of the time, but averages 15 steps per task when the expert trajectory is 4.
**Task**: How do you evaluate, and what would you change?
**Sample Answer**: TSR looks great but Path Efficiency is 4/15 = 0.27. I would compute a combined score like `0.6 * TSR + 0.4 * PE` to make the inefficiency visible in the headline. I would inspect the trajectory: is the agent over-reflecting (running the same tool twice to "be sure"), or thrashing between tools without committing? Likely fixes: tighten the planner's stop condition, cap max steps at 6, or add a "are you done?" self-check that fires every 3 steps. I would also report cost-per-success — at 15 steps the token bill may be 4x what is needed, which alone justifies the fix.

**Scenario**: Tool Selection Accuracy is 95%, but Task Success Rate is only 60%.
**Task**: Debug this. Where is the failure?
**Sample Answer**: TSA being high means the agent knows *which* tool to use, so the failure is downstream. Three suspects: (1) **argument extraction** — the agent passes wrong args. Check TAC. (2) **tool execution** — the API is failing or returning bad data. Check Tool Execution Success. (3) **reasoning over observations** — the agent gets correct results but misinterprets them. Inspect a sample of failed trajectories and bucket failures. If TAC is low, improve arg schemas or add validation. If TES is low, the environment, not the agent, is broken. If both are fine, the planner LLM is the bug — switch to a stronger model or add a "summarize observation" step.

**Scenario**: Your coding agent passes SWE-bench Verified at 40% but fails 70% of your company's internal Jira tickets.
**Task**: Why the gap, and how do you fix the eval?
**Sample Answer**: SWE-bench is open-source Python repos with existing test suites. Your tickets are likely private codebases, multiple languages, no test coverage, and require domain context the agent doesn't have. The benchmark doesn't reflect your distribution. Fix: build an internal eval set — sample 50–100 resolved tickets, capture the agent's PR vs the human PR, and judge with a rubric (does it compile, pass CI, match reviewer intent?). Re-run weekly. Also instrument failure types: "couldn't find the file" vs "edited the wrong function" vs "didn't understand the business logic." Each needs a different intervention (better retrieval, stronger planner, domain docs in context).

**Scenario**: You ship an agent to production. Offline TSR was 88%. After a week, production TSR measured from traces is 62%.
**Task**: What happened, and how do you investigate?
**Sample Answer**: Three common causes. (1) **Distribution shift** — real user tasks are harder, longer, or weirder than the eval set. (2) **Environment drift** — an API the agent depends on changed, or rate limits kicked in. (3) **Non-determinism** — eval was on a single run; production is on many. Investigate: pull 100 failed traces, bucket by failure type, compare to eval distribution. Check TES for tool/API failures. Check whether failures cluster by user segment or time-of-day (rate limits). Re-run a sample of failed production tasks offline — if they now pass, the issue was environment or latency; if they still fail, eval coverage was incomplete.

**Next**: Open `05-multi-agent-evaluation.md` to extend these ideas to systems of multiple coordinating agents — where new metrics like **role effectiveness** and **coordination overhead** enter the picture.
